scenes.title: Clustered Index
scenes.narration: A clustered index defines the physical order in which a table's rows are actually stored on disk.

scenes.title: Defining characteristics
bullets: It sets the physical storage order of the rows
Its leaf level is the table data itself, not a separate copy
A table can have only one clustered index
scenes.narration: A clustered index dictates the physical order of the rows on disk. Its leaf level is the table data itself rather than a separate structure, so there is nowhere else for the row to live. Because rows can only be sorted one way physically, each table can have just one clustered index.

scenes.title: Creating one
scenes.code:
-- The primary key is usually the clustered index
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT,
    order_date DATE,
    total      NUMERIC(10,2)
);

-- Range scans on the clustered key are efficient
SELECT order_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE order_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000;
scenes.narration: Most engines make the primary key the clustered index by default, so here order_id defines the storage order. Because the rows are physically sorted by order_id, a range query like this one reads a contiguous block of the table. The engine seeks to the start of the range and scans forward without jumping around the disk.

scenes.title: Clustered index trade-offs

left.title: Strengths
points: Very fast range scans on the key
No extra lookup to reach row data
Sorted output for free on the key

right.title: Costs
points: Inserts in random key order cause page splits
Only one clustered index per table
Wide clustering keys bloat every other index

scenes.narration: The clustered index makes range scans and ordered reads on the key very cheap, since the data is already sorted and no extra lookup is needed. The costs are that random-order inserts trigger page splits, you only get one per table, and a wide clustering key inflates every non-clustered index that references it.

scenes.title: How a lookup travels the tree
steps: Start at the root of the B-tree
Arrive at the leaf, which holds the full row
Return the row directly — no second read
scenes.narration: A clustered-index lookup starts at the root of the B-tree and navigates down through intermediate pages. It arrives at a leaf page that holds the full row rather than a pointer. The row is returned directly, so there is no second read to fetch the data.

scenes.text: In engines like InnoDB every table is clustered on its primary key, so choose a narrow, ever-increasing key to keep inserts cheap and lookups fast.
scenes.narration: In storage engines like InnoDB every table is clustered on its primary key, so pick a narrow, steadily increasing key to keep inserts cheap and lookups fast.
